description: MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning) is a benchmark of 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines (Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering) across 30 subjects and 183 subfields. It features 30 highly heterogeneous image types and interleaved text-image inputs, designed to evaluate expert-level perception and reasoning with domain-specific knowledge in large multimodal models.
name: MMMU
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in the relevant majors across 30 subjects. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent a wide range of experts in the corresponding 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human expert performance was measured on the 900-question validation set: Expert (Worst) achieved 76.2%, Expert (Medium) 82.6%, and Expert (Best) 88.6% accuracy. Error analysis was conducted on 150 randomly sampled GPT-4V error cases by expert annotators who identified root causes: 35% perceptual errors, 29% lack of knowledge, 26% reasoning errors, 4% textual understanding errors, 3% rejection to answer, 2% annotation errors, 1% answer extraction errors.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators (over 50 university students specializing in the relevant majors) collected multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources, creating new questions where necessary. They were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoid data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution, and select questions without immediately available answers to mitigate data contamination. Questions were then reviewed for duplicates (using lexical overlap and source URL similarity), checked for format and typos by co-authors, and categorized into four difficulty levels. Approximately 10% of problems classified as very easy were excluded.
rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. The benchmark focuses on college-level subjects, which may not fully represent the breadth of tasks required for Expert AGI. Some subjects (e.g., law and linguistics) were excluded because it was difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems, potentially skewing subject coverage.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were manually collected by a team of over 50 college students (including co-authors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials. The collection process involved three stages: (1) selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted; (2) recruiting university students specializing in these majors to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary; (3) annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations and to select questions without immediately available answers to avoid data contamination.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Multimodal questions sourced from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, and online resources across 30 subjects and 183 subfields. The raw collection resulted in approximately 13K questions before quality filtering.
rai:dataLimitations: The manual curation process may carry biases. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. There lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and "90th percentile of skilled adults," nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Two-step data cleaning: (1) lexical overlap and source URL similarity were used to identify potential duplicate problems, which were then reviewed by authors to eliminate duplications; (2) problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format. In a third stage, problems were categorized into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard), and approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded from the benchmark.
rai:dataSocialImpact: MMMU is designed to monitor progress towards Expert AGI, which is defined as AI reaching "at least 90th percentile of skilled adults" in a broad range of tasks. Achieving Expert AGI could lead to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. The benchmark aims to provide a shared operationalizable definition for measuring progress towards this milestone.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning; benchmarking progress towards Expert AGI; stimulating development of next-generation multimodal foundation models.

evidence.name: We introduce MMMU : a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning.
evidence.description: MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.

evidence.rai:dataLimitations: MMMU , like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI [57]. However, we argue that strong performance on this benchmark should be a necessary criterion for an Expert AGI system.

evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Level 3, or Expert AGI, marks a critical milestone. It denotes an AI system that reaches "at least 90th percentile of skilled adults" in a broad range of tasks, thus starting to achieve "the substitution threshold for machine intelligence in lieu of human labor" for many industries, leading to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. Therefore, it is of both intellectual and societal importance to closely monitor the progress towards Expert AGI.
